questions.question: What paper introduced multi-agent debate and what conference was it presented at?
options: Yao et al., NeurIPS 2023
Du et al., ICML 2024 (arXiv:2305.14325) — 'Society of Minds'
Shinn et al., NeurIPS 2023
Zhou et al., ICML 2024
questions.explanation: Du et al. introduced multi-agent debate in 'Society of Minds' (arXiv:2305.14325), presented at ICML 2024. Original experiments used N=3 debaters, R=2 rounds due to token cost.

questions.question: What is the debate protocol?
options: One agent proposes, others vote, majority wins
N model instances independently propose answers, then over R rounds each reads others' proposals and critiques them, updating answers until convergence
Agents take turns proposing and the final agent's answer is used
All agents share memory and produce one joint answer
questions.explanation: Multi-agent debate: N model instances independently propose answers, then over R rounds each model reads the others' proposals, critiques them, and updates their own answer. After R rounds, the convergent answer is returned.

questions.question: What is a sparse topology in multi-agent debate and what is its advantage?
options: A topology with fewer agents; advantage is lower cost
Agents read only a subset of peers (star, ring, hub-and-spoke); can match full-mesh accuracy at lower token cost
Agents that skip some rounds; advantage is faster convergence
Agents that communicate asynchronously; advantage is lower latency
questions.explanation: Sparse topology means each debater sees only a subset of peers rather than all of them. Research showed sparse topologies (star, ring, hub-and-spoke) can match full-mesh accuracy at lower token cost — a star with N=5 uses 12 critique ops vs 60 for full mesh.

questions.question: What is the 'convergence collapse' failure mode in multi-agent debate?
options: The debate fails to converge within R rounds
All agents converge on the same wrong answer early, eliminating the diversity that makes debate valuable
One agent becomes dominant and others stop contributing
The debate produces multiple conflicting answers with no consensus
questions.explanation: Convergence collapse: all agents converge on the first wrong answer put forward by one agent. Mitigation: require disagreement in round 1, use diverse prompts and/or different model families to prevent homogenization.

questions.question: When does debate NOT help compared to a single model?
options: When accuracy is the only concern
When latency-sensitive or cost-sensitive, or for simple factual lookups where single-model lookup is cheaper
When the task involves rule-following
When using frontier models
questions.explanation: Debate hurts relative to single-model when: latency is tight (N×R serial rounds), cost is constrained (N×R tokens per question), or the task is a simple factual lookup where one retrieval is cheaper than five parallel debates.

questions.question: What finding from Du et al. shows the benefit of model heterogeneity in debate?
options: More agents always produce better results
Cross-model combinations (ChatGPT + Bard together) beat single-model debates
Smaller models debate better than larger ones
Models from the same provider reach consensus faster
questions.explanation: Du et al. found that cross-model combinations beat single-model debates: ChatGPT + Bard together outperformed either model debating with itself. This is why diverse prompts and/or different model families are recommended to prevent prompt homogenization.
